summary: Describes using the AES Galois Message Authentication Code (GMAC) in IPsec ESP and AH to provide data origin authentication without confidentiality. GMAC is based on the Galois/Counter Mode of operation, so it can reuse hardware built for that mode. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a tamper-proof seal on a letter. The seal shows who sent it and that nobody changed it, but the letter can still be read by anyone along the way.

subtitle: How IPsec can prove who sent a packet, without encrypting it, by running AES-GCM with an empty message.

tldr.problem: Some IPsec users want proof that a packet came from the right sender and was not altered, but do not want or need confidentiality.
tldr.mechanism: AES-GMAC is AES-GCM with a zero-length plaintext, so everything to be protected goes in as additional authenticated data and only the 16-octet authentication tag is kept. It is defined for ESP as a combined mode called ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC and for AH as AUTH_AES_GMAC.
tldr.outcome: It adds 8 octets of IV and 16 octets of ICV per packet, and must be used with automated key management such as IKE so that a nonce and key pair is never reused.

today: RFC 4543 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006. The metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why GMAC for IPsec
sections.content:
RFC 4543 describes the use of AES-GMAC for data origin authentication in ESP (RFC 4303) and AH (RFC 4302). The two methods are named ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC for ESP and AUTH_AES_GMAC for AH.

ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC is a companion to AES Galois/Counter Mode ESP (RFC 4106), which gives authentication and confidentiality. The new method is for cases where confidentiality is not wanted. The RFC says the extra cost of implementing it, for anyone who already has AES-GCM-ESP, is small. It does not cover the details of GCM or GMAC themselves, which are left to the GCM specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want a sealed envelope that proves who sent it, but you do not mind if people can read the letter. This document says how to make that kind of seal for internet packets.

sections.title: What AES-GMAC Is
sections.content:
GMAC is a block cipher mode that provides data origin authentication. It is defined from the GCM authenticated encryption operation, which takes a secret key, an initialization vector (IV), a plaintext and additional authenticated data (AAD), and returns a ciphertext and an authentication tag.

GMAC is the special case of GCM in which the plaintext has a length of zero. The empty ciphertext is ignored, so the only output is the authentication tag.

To avoid confusion with the IV fields in packets, the RFC calls the GMAC IV input a nonce. The same nonce and key combination MUST NOT be used more than once, because reuse destroys the security guarantees. For that reason implementations MUST use an automated key management system such as IKE (version one or two) rather than statically configured keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a machine that normally scrambles a message and stamps it. GMAC feeds it a blank page, so all you get back is the stamp. Each stamp must use a fresh number, or the trick stops being safe.

sections.title: GMAC in ESP
sections.content:
For ESP, AES-GMAC is defined as a "combined mode" algorithm rather than an integrity algorithm. It is called ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC to stress that it does no encryption and gives no confidentiality. The RFC's reasoning is that ESP lets only encryption transforms place an IV in the Payload field, so defining GMAC as an encryption transform solves that and lets it benefit from the same pipelining as GCM.

Like other combined modes it is registered in IKEv2 as a Type 1 encryption transform. It MUST NOT be combined with another ESP encryption transform in the same encapsulation. If confidentiality is wanted, GCM ESP (RFC 4106) SHOULD be used instead.

An explicit IV sits at the start of the ESP Payload. It MUST be eight octets long and MUST NOT repeat for a given key. A counter is the natural choice, but any method that guarantees uniqueness, such as an LFSR, is allowed, and the sender needs no coordination with the receiver.

The nonce handed to GMAC is a four-octet salt followed by the eight-octet IV. The salt is fixed when the security association is set up and stays constant for its life. It SHOULD be unpredictable but need not be secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries its own fresh number, like a ticket number. The sender can pick the numbers any way it likes, as long as it never hands out the same one twice.

sections.title: What Is Authenticated and What Is Added
sections.content:
Integrity and origin authentication cover the SPI, the (Extended) Sequence Number, the Authenticated Payload, the Padding, the Pad Length and the Next Header fields. They are all fed in as AAD. There is one AAD format for 32-bit sequence numbers and one for 64-bit extended sequence numbers. Which is used is decided by the SA management protocol; with IKEv2 it is negotiated through Transform Type 5, and ESP defaults to 64-bit extended sequence numbers if nothing is negotiated.

The ICV is just the AES-GMAC authentication tag, and it MUST NOT be truncated, so it is 16 octets long. The IV adds 8 octets and the ICV adds 16 octets to the packet. Apart from the 10 to 13 bytes taken by the SPI, sequence number, padding, pad length and next header (with minimal padding), these are the only sources of packet expansion.

ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC is not AES-GCM-ESP with encryption turned off. In AES-GCM-ESP the AAD is only the SPI and sequence number and the ESP Payload is the plaintext. Here the AAD holds the SPI, sequence number and payload, and the plaintext is empty. The ICV computations are similar because of the structure of the GHASH function.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal covers almost everything on the packet: the address label, the page number, the contents and the padding at the end. Nothing is hidden, but nothing can be changed without breaking the seal.

sections.title: GMAC in AH
sections.content:
In AUTH_AES_GMAC the AH Authentication Data field holds the IV and the authentication tag. Unlike usual AH, this field holds both an input to the algorithm (the IV) and its output (the tag). No padding is needed, because the length is a multiple of 64 bits.

The IV and ICV are as described for ESP: eight octets and 16 octets. The nonce is built the same way, and the AAD is the authenticated data defined in Section 3.1 of RFC 4302.
sections.plainLanguage: In this version the sender writes the ticket number and the stamp side by side in one box on the packet, so the receiver has everything needed to check it.

sections.title: IKE Conventions
sections.content:
The RFC does not define AES-GMAC for IKE Phase 1; that would need a separate specification. Implementations SHOULD use a Phase 1 cipher at least as strong as AES-GMAC, and AES-CBC (RFC 3602) with the same AES key size is RECOMMENDED.

AES-GMAC works with any of the three AES key lengths. For AH each key length has its own integrity transform identifier and the IKE Key Length attribute MUST NOT be used. For ESP there is a single encryption transform identifier, and the Key Length attribute MUST be used with a value of 128, 192 or 256.

The keying material (KEYMAT) must be four octets longer than the AES key, and the extra four octets become the salt. That gives 20 octets for a 128-bit key, 28 for 192-bit and 36 for 256-bit. The IANA values are 9, 10 and 11 for AUTH_AES_128_GMAC, AUTH_AES_192_GMAC and AUTH_AES_256_GMAC (integrity, type 3), and 21 for ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC (encryption, type 1).
sections.plainLanguage: The secret key and the salt come out of the same batch of random material that the two computers agree on. The salt is just the last few bytes of that batch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that both this method and AES-GCM-ESP are secure even though they cover different data. In ESP the IV is not part of the AAD, which is fine because the IV only feeds the GMAC IV. In AH the IV is in the AAD, which is also fine because GMAC stays secure even against an adversary who can manipulate both the IV and the message. GMAC is described as provably secure under standard cryptographic assumptions: a break of GMAC implies a break of the underlying block cipher.

The most important rule is that the IV never repeats for a given key. IKE establishes separate keys for the two traffic directions. If some other mechanism gives only one key for both, the peers could choose the same IVs, so implementations MUST ensure the two peers use different salt values.

Implementations MUST generate a fresh key before processing 2^64 blocks of data with a given key. This limit cannot be reached with 32-bit sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The one big rule is never to use the same ticket number twice with the same key. Follow that, and breaking the seal would be as hard as breaking AES itself.

fields.name: Salt
fields.desc: Four octets fixed for the life of the security association; unpredictable but not secret.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: Eight octets carried in the packet; must not repeat for a given key.
